idiom_name: static nested Builder class + build() calling the product's private constructor
implementation_notes: Java has neither named nor default parameters, so the builder is the standard hand-written replacement: a static nested Builder whose constructor receives the required fields, one method per optional field returning this, and build() copying the accumulated values into the product's private constructor after checking the invariants - the product itself stays immutable with final fields. Bloch notes explicitly that the idiom exists to simulate named optional parameters, which is why languages that have them (Kotlin, Python, Scala, C# records) rarely need it. For hierarchies use a parallel builder hierarchy with the self-referential generic (abstract static class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> plus self()) so subclass builders keep returning their own type.
code_sketch:
NutritionFacts f = new NutritionFacts.Builder(240, 8)   // required fields
        .calories(100)
        .sodium(35)
        .carbohydrate(27)
        .build();                                       // copies + validates
// Builder is a static nested class; the all-args constructor is private.
pitfalls: build() must copy collection arguments (List.copyOf(...)) and re-check multi-field invariants on the copied values, or the supposedly immutable product can be mutated through a retained reference.
Chained subclass builders need the self-referential generic plus self(); without it a subclass method returns the base builder and the chain stops compiling midway.
A builder constructor that omits required fields defers the failure to a runtime IllegalStateException: keep required values as constructor parameters or move to a staged builder.

variants.name: Generated builders (Lombok @Builder, Immutables, AutoValue)
variants.implementation_notes: Annotation processors write the boilerplate: Lombok's @Builder on a class or constructor generates a nested FooBuilder with one chained setter per field, a static builder() factory, toBuilder() for copies and @Singular adders that compact collections; Immutables and AutoValue go further and generate the whole immutable value type plus builder from an abstract class or interface, tracking unset required attributes with bit masks and offering strict and staged builder modes. Reach for the hand-written form when the build cannot carry an annotation processor, since Lombok runs inside javac and constrains toolchain and IDE upgrades.
pitfalls: Generated builders are ordinary mutable objects by default and a field can be set twice; enable strict/staged modes (@Value.Style(strictBuilder = true, stagedBuilder = true)) when the API must reject that.
Lombok rewrites the class inside javac, so the processor version must match the compiler, and @Builder on a class with an explicit constructor silently changes which constructor it targets.
